mcqs.question: A request fans out to 100 independent backend calls, each with a 1% chance of hitting its own p99 tail latency. Why does the overall request's typical latency end up dominated by tail latency rather than average latency?
options: Because with 100 independent calls, the chance that at least one hits its slow tail is high (roughly 63%), so the aggregate request is often waiting on someone's tail case
Because average latency doesn't apply to fan-out requests at all
Because only the very first backend call's latency matters for the aggregate
Because tail latency and average latency are always identical at high fan-out
mcqs.explanation: With many independent calls each having a small chance of being slow, the probability that at least one of them is slow compounds quickly — roughly 63% at 100 calls with 1% each — so the aggregate is frequently waiting on someone's tail. Average latency still applies to each individual call; it's just not what the aggregate outcome tracks once fan-out is high.

mcqs.question: You set a hedging delay of 1ms for a call whose typical latency is 20ms. What's the likely consequence?
options: Most requests trigger a duplicate even though the original would have returned fine shortly after, roughly doubling load for little latency benefit
Hedging will never fire since 1ms is too short to ever be reached
This delay is ideal regardless of the call's actual latency distribution
Tail latency will be completely eliminated with no added cost
mcqs.explanation: A delay far shorter than typical latency means nearly every request hedges, since the first response almost never arrives that fast — doubling request volume without meaningfully improving latency for the typical case. It's not too short to be reached, and hedging always has some cost, whatever the delay.

mcqs.question: What's the key difference in when hedged requests and plain retries are triggered?
options: Retries fire proactively before any failure; hedging only fires after an explicit failure
Hedging fires after a short delay whether or not the first call has failed yet; retries only fire after the first call has actually failed or timed out
Both are triggered at exactly the same point in a request's lifecycle
Hedging is only usable for writes, while retries are only usable for reads
mcqs.explanation: Hedging is proactive — it fires on a timer regardless of whether the first call eventually would have succeeded — while retries are reactive, only happening once a failure is confirmed. The two aren't triggered at the same point, and neither is restricted to only reads or only writes as described.

mcqs.question: A team hedges a "append this event to the log" call, which is not idempotent. What risk does this introduce?
options: None — hedging always guarantees only one of the two attempts actually executes
The event may be appended twice, since hedging doesn't guarantee the first attempt is cancelled before completing
The call becomes automatically idempotent once hedged
Hedging only affects latency, never correctness, for any type of call
mcqs.explanation: Plain hedging doesn't guarantee cancellation of the losing attempt, so a non-idempotent write can genuinely execute twice — the same risk as a naive retry on a non-idempotent write. Hedging doesn't make a call idempotent by itself, and it clearly can affect correctness for writes, not just latency.

mcqs.question: A dependency becomes genuinely overloaded, and hedging keeps adding duplicate requests as more calls cross the hedging threshold. Without a hedging budget, what's the risk?
options: Hedging automatically throttles itself once load gets too high, so there's no real risk
A positive feedback loop where hedging adds load to an already-struggling dependency, pushing more requests into hedging and worsening the overload
The hedging delay automatically increases to compensate
This can only happen if the hedging delay is set too long, never too short
mcqs.explanation: Without a cap, hedging can amplify an overload it should be mitigating — more slow requests trigger more hedges, adding more load, in a self-reinforcing spiral. Hedging doesn't self-throttle or auto-adjust its delay on its own; a hedging budget is the deliberate fix for exactly this, and the risk isn't tied to one specific delay setting.
